speaker: Kimi K3
text: Answering the client's open questions: a US IPO with $10 isn't really possible since retail IPO allocations need a brokerage with IPO access and minimums, and Indian IPOs need a full lot that typically runs well above your Rs 10,000, so IPOs can't be your 10x route. On Reliance via Zerodha delivery, the floor data shows the round trip costs about 0.38% (Rs 38 on Rs 10,000 including the flat DP charge), plus 20% short-term capital-gains tax if you sell within a year. On the spotlight, NVDA's fundamentals back Nemotron's momentum read: revenue up 105.9% YoY last quarter with 66.2% operating margins and 58 of 61 analysts at buy or better, though insiders sold $1.37B in six months with zero buys, which is the one fundamental crack I'd flag.

text: If you try to snag an IPO with a $10 retail order you’ll hit the minimum allotment wall – most IPOs require a full lot (₹10,000‑₹50,000 in India, a few hundred dollars in the US) and a broker that offers IPO access, so a $10 stake won’t get you a share.  For a Reliance purchase on Zerodha’s delivery desk the round‑trip cost on a ₹10,000 order is about ₹38 (0.38 % of the trade) – that covers STT, exchange fee, SEBI, stamp duty, GST and the DP charge.  If you sell within a year the 20 % short‑term capital‑gain tax will be applied to the profit.  Buying $10 of NVDA fractional shares now would give you roughly 0.0428 shares; at the current 25.2 % yearly CAGR that would grow to about $12.50 in a year – still far from the 10× target, but it’s a low‑cost, low‑risk way to stay in the chip play.  If you’re also interested in cars and battery makers, look at EV names like Tata Motors (TATAMOTORS.NS), Mahindra & Mahindra (M&M.NS) and battery firms such as Exide Industries (EXIDEIND.NS) or Amara Raja (AMARAJARAJA.NS) – all are listed on NSE/BSE and can be bought in whole shares with the same delivery charges you’d pay for Reliance.
